text: (a) Πνευματικὸς τόμος. Missa hæc epistola, sive liber dogmaticus ad Stephanum Dorensem episcopum, fidei catholicæ cum archiepiscopo suo Sophronio adversus Monothelitas strenuum defensorem, inque eam rem ab eodem Romam missum, ubi orthodoxorum dogmatum fundamenta exsisterent, inquit idem Sophronius egregia illa suggestione, quæ exstat in concil. Later. sub Martino I, secretar. seu consult. 2. Cumque Maximus hanc Romam mittat, argumento est, sub exordium fere novi dogmatis missam esse, et cum solum edita esset Heracliana, seu magis Sergiana Ecthesis, in quam unam invehitur, nec Constantis Typus adhuc cusus esset, cujus illi Paulus, ipse in eo concilio damnatus, ac a Stephano exagitatus, auctor fuit. Tantæ ergo fidei in Stephano præcipuus incentor videatur Maximus; potuitque per eum sic Theodoro papæ innotescere, ut ei vices suas, et Conservatorium, ut vocabant, in Palæstina ac Hierosolymitana diœcesi concrederet: quo in munere suas strenue exsecutum partes, depositis, qui libellum pœnitentiæ non obtulissent, male promotis per Sergium Joppensem episcopis, ac qui fidei catholicæ scripto assensum non præbuissent, ipse in ea suggestione locuples testis exsistit. Quo et Romani antistitis mire elucet auctoritas, et sollicitudo Ecclesiarum, in causa præsertim fidei, qualis hic vertebatur, ubique terrarum vere orthodoxis spectatissima. Πρωτόθρονον Hierosolymitani throni seu sedis ac diœcesis haud obscure se Stephanus significat, sive id habebat suæ sedis privilegio, quæ esset prima et dignior usu ecclesiastico, cæteris post ipsam Hierosolymitanam sedem, sive etiam quia ipse senior episcopus erat, quomodo Africa primates suos agnoscebat; aut denique quod Conservatoriam a sede apostolica acceperat, vacante sede Hierosolymitana per Sophronii obitum. Hanc porro epistolam habuit etiam cod. Em. card. Barberini, ex qua plurima mutuata sexta synodus, præsertim Agatho in sua suggestione, ex cujus sensu peracta omnia in illo concilio, quæ ad fidei negotium spectabant, ut ejus triumphi præcipuæ partes Maximi fuisse videantur, ac gloria prostratæ Monothelitarum hæresis, tum Romæ Martino papa, tum Constantinopoli Agathone.
anchorLine: Πνευματικὸς τόμος (α) καὶ δογματικὸς, ἀπεδεικνὺς
en: (a) "Πνευματικὸς τόμος" (Spiritual Tome). This epistle, or dogmatic book, was sent to Stephen, bishop of Dora, as a stalwart defender of the catholic faith together with his archbishop Sophronius against the Monothelites, and was sent by him to Rome for that purpose, where the foundations of orthodox doctrines were to be found, as the same Sophronius says in that excellent suggestio which is extant in the Lateran council under Martin I, in the secretarium or consultation 2. Since Maximus sends it to Rome, it is evidence that it was composed near the beginning of the new doctrine, and when only the Heraclian, or rather Sergian, Ecthesis had been published, against which alone he inveighs, and Constans's Typos had not yet been struck, of which Paul, himself condemned in that council and attacked by Stephen, was the author. So Maximus seems the chief instigator of such great faith in Stephen; and through him he could thus become known to Pope Theodore, so that he entrusted to him his own vicarial powers and the Conservatorium, as they called it, in Palestine and the diocese of Jerusalem. In that office he vigorously carried out his duties: he deposed those who had not offered a petition of penance and had been wrongly promoted by Sergius of Joppa as bishops, and those who had not given assent to the written statement of the catholic faith; he himself stands as a reliable witness in that suggestio. By this the authority of the Roman pontiff shines out wonderfully, and the care of the Churches, especially in a cause of faith such as was being treated here, most conspicuous everywhere among the truly orthodox. Stephen indicates not obscurely that he is "Πρωτόθρονος" of the throne, or see and diocese, of Jerusalem, whether he had it by the privilege of his see, which was first and more worthy by ecclesiastical custom, the others coming after the see of Jerusalem itself; or also because he was himself the senior bishop, as Africa recognized its primates; or finally because he had received the Conservatoria from the apostolic see, the see of Jerusalem being vacant through Sophronius's death. This epistle, moreover, Cardinal Barberini's codex also contained, from which the sixth synod borrowed very much, especially Agatho in his suggestio, from whose sense everything in that council that concerned the matter of faith was carried out, so that the principal part of its triumph seems to have been Maximus's, and the glory of the overthrow of the Monothelite heresy, both at Rome under Pope Martin and at Constantinople under Agatho.

en: "To the borders of Tyre." In that suggestio of Agatho (the reading is) τὰ μεθόρια (the border-lands), as also in the vulgate Greek copies. What stood a little further on, "περιπατεῖ ὁ Ἰησοῦς" (Jesus walks), is emended to "περιεπάτει" (walked): because the sacred text so has it and the sequence of the narrative requires it, "for he did not wish", which alone Pope Agatho cited in his own report (anaphora).

text: (c) Μὴ περὶ τοῦ κατεληλυθότος. In editis Gregorii, ut et in act. illa 4 sextæ synodi, est παρὰ, ut et statim sequentibus, ὡς παρὰ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου. Ipse certe, et de se ipse Christus loquebatur, qui e cœlo descenderit; quo videtur insinuari sensus formalis, ut in sua ipse persona loquatur, non communiter in persona hominum, et solum per arrogationem, tribuendo sibi quæ humani generis communia sunt. Non video quid sibi velit, qui Morelianæ editioni marg. ascripsit, ἴσ. παρὰ σοῦ. Nihil certe, quidquid est, videtur frugi.
anchorLine: μὴ περὶ τοῦ κατεληλυθότος (c) ταῦτα ἐλέγετο, εἶ-
en: (c) "Not about the one who had come down." In the editions of Gregory, as also in act 4 of the sixth synod, it reads παρὰ, as also in what follows at once, ὡς παρὰ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου. Surely Christ himself was speaking of himself also, he who had come down from heaven; by which a formal sense seems to be hinted, that he speaks in his own person, not in the common way in the person of men, and only by arrogation, attributing to himself what is common to the human race. I do not see what he means who wrote in the margin of the Morellian edition, 'perhaps παρὰ σοῦ'. Whatever it is, it certainly seems of no use.

text: (d) Τὸ συναφὲς τῆς ἑαυτοῦ πρὸς τὸν Πατέρα θεότητος. Mendose Latina act. illa 4 ejusdem synodi, Ostendit conjunctionem propriæ divinitatis Patrem, pro, cum Patre. Pleraque hujus epistolæ extant in illa suggestione Agathonis, etsi quædam paulo brevius in ea sunt relata: ut in sequenti loco Chrysost. omissum illud, Ὁρᾷς πῶς καὶ τὴν προτέραν αὐτοῦ ἡλικίαν προανεφώνησεν: ubi male Ducæus plurali numero, προανεφώνησαν, prænuntiarint, cum sermo sit de uno Isaia, sic de Christi priore ætate vaticinato. Illud etiam ejus postea, ἐπὶ τῆς δυνάμεως in qua ait Chrysostom. Catholicos ponere, quod Filius sit unum cum Patre, cum hæretici ponerent in voluntate, in majestate, liberius est: non enim ea voce Græci majestatem significant, sed virtutem ac potentiam, quæ ipsa naturæ index est.
anchorLine: ἔδειξε τὸ συναφὲς τῆς ἑαυτοῦ πρὸς τὸν Πατέρα Θεότη-τος (d), ἧς οὐδεμία θελήματός ἐστι διαφορά, διὰ τὴν
en: (d) "The connection of his own divinity with the Father." The Latin in act 4 of the same synod is faulty: 'Ostendit conjunctionem propriae divinitatis Patrem' for 'cum Patre'. Most of this epistle stands in that suggestio of Agatho, although some things are reported there more briefly; as in the following passage of Chrysostom the omitted phrase 'Ὁρᾷς πῶς καὶ τὴν προτέραν αὐτοῦ ἡλικίαν προανεφώνησεν' (see how he also foretold his earlier age); where Ducaeus wrongly puts it in the plural, προανεφώνησαν, 'prenuntiarint', though the discourse is about Isaiah alone, who prophesied thus of Christ's earlier age. Also his later phrase, ἐπὶ τῆς δυνάμεως, in which Chrysostom says Catholics place that the Son is one with the Father, whereas heretics placed it in will: 'in majestate' is too free a rendering, for the Greeks do not mean majesty by that word but virtue and power, which itself is the sign of nature.

text: suggestio, nec male Latina, docebatur a Deo Verbo gestata caro, hoc deinceps minime pati. At certe pessime, nihilque ecclesiastice Bonaventura Vulcan. Considera quod caro, quæ a Verbo gestabatur, non bene ad hoc ferendum affecta erat. Plane docebatur sic humano more indulgere affectibus, ad ostensionem assumptæ humanitatis, ut in eis non diutius moraretur, sed fortiori animo hos compesceret, ut cum infremuit in Lazaro, quasi cohibendo naturalem animi miserantis motum. Sic et in passione, Verumtamen non mea, sed tua voluntas fiat.
anchorLine: Θεοῦ Λόγου μηκέτι τοῦτο πάσχειν (e) [on p-0098]
en: ...suggestio [of Agatho], and not badly in Latin: 'the flesh borne by God the Word was taught henceforth not to suffer this.' But Bonaventura Vulcanius (renders it) very badly and in no ecclesiastical manner: 'Consider that the flesh, which was borne by the Word, was not well disposed to bear this.' Plainly it was being taught to indulge the affections in a human way, to show the humanity assumed, so as not to linger long in them but to restrain them with a stronger spirit, as when he groaned at Lazarus, as if checking the natural movement of a pitying soul. So too in the passion: 'Nevertheless not my will but thine be done.'

text: (f) Ἡ αὐτὴ ἐνέργεια ἐκ διαφόρου ἐστὶν οὐσίας. Plane luxatio est, reddiditque Maximus, διαφόρου ἐξουσίας, quod Ambrosii textus habet: Quemadmodum eadem operatio diversæ esset potestatis? Ambrosii voce, non admodum propria, motus, ut et Græcam adhiberet, ei respondentem, ipsam non satis ex usu philosophico; meliusque Agathonis suggestionis interpr., ἡ αὐτὴ ἐνέργεια διαφόρου
anchorLine: ἡ αὐτὴ ἐνέργεια ἐκ διαφόρου ἐστὶν οὐσίας (f); μὴ
en: (f) "The same operation is of a different essence." This is plainly a dislocation, and Maximus rendered it "of a different authority" (διαφόρου ἐξουσίας), which is what Ambrose's text has: "How could the same operation be of different power?" Moved by Ambrose's wording, which is not quite proper, to supply a Greek one corresponding to it, itself not sufficiently in philosophical usage; and Agatho's suggestio translates better: "ἡ αὐτὴ ἐνέργεια διαφόρου" [the note breaks off here at the foot of the page and continues on p-0100].

text: ἐστὶν δυνάμεως. Sic quoque sequentibus Maximus vocem ἐξουσίας usurpavit, Μίαν εἶναι τὴν θέλησιν, μίαν τὴν ἐνέργειαν, κατὰ μίαν καὶ τὴν αὐτὴν ἐξουσίαν προαγομένην. Ἐξουσία in illis magis proprie dicatur, quæ γνωμικῶς, ex arbitrio et sententia, quam quæ φυσικῶς (natura scilicet) volumus ac operamur. Quod etiam paulo post sequitur in Leonis auctoritate, ἐνεργεῖ ἐν ἑκατέρᾳ μορφῇ, ipsum quoque emend. ex Latinis, ἐνεργεῖ ἑκατέρα μορφή· agit utraque forma; quo etiam modo in sequentibus habetur, ubi eædem auctoritates breviter perstringuntur. Forte scripserit Maximus ac reddiderit, ἐνεργεῖ γὰρ ἐν ἑκατέρᾳ μορφῇ· quod nihil sensu a Latinis diversum, sed paulo elegantius redditum. In ea Leonis epistola, qualem Græcam repræsentavit Gerardus Vossius, multæ sunt variæ lectiones, quidquid diligentiæ adhibitum, ut ipsa pura, qualis a Leone edita erat, ubique in Ecclesiis haberetur, quasi veræ fidei tessera. Ipsa Leonis locutio visa confundentibus longe durior, quasi divisioni in specie favens: ipsa tamen necessaria ad ipsorum magis elidendam impietatem. Lenius illi habuissent, quod ita hic repræsentatur; ac num illorum aliquis (vel ipse antiquarius) sic lenire voluit? Haud certe, putem, ipse Maximus. Rem probant quæ hic, pluresque in actis sextæ synodi exstant, eorum auctoritates.
anchorLine: ἡ αὐτὴ ἐνέργεια ἐκ διαφόρου ἐστὶν οὐσίας (f) [on p-0099]
en: ...[Agatho's reading] ἐστὶν δυνάμεως ('is of power'). So too in what follows Maximus used the word ἐξουσία: "that there is one will, one operation, according to one and the same authority going forth." In those passages ἐξουσία is more properly said of what we will and do γνωμικῶς (by choice and judgment) than of what we do φυσικῶς (naturally). The same appears a little later in the authority of Leo: ἐνεργεῖ ἐν ἑκατέρᾳ μορφῇ, which too is to be emended from the Latin to ἐνεργεῖ ἑκατέρα μορφή, 'each form acts'; it is so also in what follows, where the same authorities are briefly touched on. Perhaps Maximus wrote and rendered ἐνεργεῖ γὰρ ἐν ἑκατέρᾳ μορφῇ, which is in no way different in sense from the Latin, but rendered a little more elegantly. In that epistle of Leo, as Gerardus Vossius presented it in Greek, there are many variant readings, whatever care was applied to keep it pure, as it was issued by Leo, in the Churches everywhere, as the token of the true faith. Leo's very phrasing seemed far harsher to the confounders, as if favouring division in kind; yet it was needed all the more to crush their impiety. They would have had it milder, as it is represented here; and did one of them (or the copyist himself) wish to soften it thus? Surely not, I think, Maximus himself. The matter is proved by what is here, and by more in the acts of the sixth synod, their authorities.

text: (g) Ἐν τῷ ἐπιγεγραμμένῳ, Αὐτὴν ἐπιφάνειαν. In Agathonis suggest. aliter et melius, Εἰς τὰ ἐπιφάνια τῆς ἐνανθρωπήσεως τοῦ Θεοῦ Λόγου: qui sit ipse libri seu orationis titulus; quod vero habet Maximi epistola, ejus initium. Plene itaque scripserit Maximus: Ἐν τῷ ἐπιγεγραμμένῳ λόγῳ εἰς τὰ ἐπιφάνια τῆς ἐνανθρωπήσεως τοῦ Θεοῦ Λόγου, οὗ ἡ ἀρχή, Αὐτὴν ἐπιφάνειαν. Sic passim breviarium auctorum scripta antiquarii, sæpe etiam nullo judicio.
anchorLine: ἐν τῷ ἐπιγεγραμμένῳ· Αὐτὴν ἐπιφάνειαν (g) τὴν ἔνσαρκον τοῦ Θεοῦ.
en: (g) "In the one entitled: Autên epiphaneian." In Agatho's suggestio, otherwise and better: "Εἰς τὰ ἐπιφάνια τῆς ἐνανθρωπήσεως τοῦ Θεοῦ Λόγου" (On the Epiphany of the Incarnation of God the Word), which is the title itself of the book or oration; what Maximus's epistle has is its beginning. So Maximus will have written in full: "In the discourse entitled On the Epiphany of the Incarnation of God the Word, whose beginning is 'Autên epiphaneian'." Thus throughout the copyist abbreviates the writings of authors, often also with no judgment.

text: (h) Μίαν τὴν γνῶσιν. Sic etiam act. 10 sextæ synodi. Μία γὰρ ἡ γνῶσις ἐπὶ Χριστοῦ, καθάπερ καὶ ἡ ἐνέργεια. Nec pro φύσις obrepsit, cum sequitur, Καὶ γὰρ εἷς ἦν ὁ γινώσκων, ὥσπερ ἀμέλει καὶ ὁ ἐνεργῶν. Sic nempe Themistius, ex una operatione unam Christi inferebat scientiam, uti et unam voluntatem: in qua vel maxime vim faciebant sequaces Monothelitæ, tanquam ipsa duplex admitti non posset, quin esset contraria: quam unam contrarietatem, et qualis nobis inolevit ex Adæ peccato, præferebant velle a Christo excludere: quo et fraudem passus Joannes abbas, ipse auctor Honorio, ut ad eum sensum Orientalibus responderet (quæ ipsa ejus satisfactio est) necdum scilicet satis explorato pro Latinorum ingenuitate, fideique sinceritate, quid iidem Orientales adversum fidei in una illa voluntate, eis asserta, molirentur, donec Sophronius, Stephanus, Maximus, aliique viri egregie catholici, Matri suppetias euntes, detectisque Syrorum insidiis, nobilissimos Romanos antistites Joannem IV, Theodorum, Martinum, ad hydram certis ictibus conficiendam, pro Romanæ sedis suprema in rebus fidei potestate, præclare animarunt; negotio demum felici exitu per Dominum, Agathonem, Leonem II et Constantinum peracto.
anchorLine: τὴν γνῶσιν (h) καὶ τὴν ἐνέργειαν, καθὰ καὶ τὴν θέλησιν.
en: (h) "Μίαν τὴν γνῶσιν" (the one knowledge). So also in act 10 of the sixth synod: "For there is one knowledge in Christ, as also one operation." Nor has φύσις crept in for it, since there follows, "For he who knows is one, just as, of course, he who operates." So Themistius inferred from one operation one knowledge of Christ, as also one will: on which point the Monothelite followers laid special stress, as though the double could not be admitted without being contrary; and that one contrariety, such as grew in us from Adam's sin, they preferred to exclude from Christ. Abbot John, himself the author for Honorius, was deceived by this fraud, so as to answer the Orientals in that sense (which is his own satisfaction), not having yet, in keeping with the frankness and sincerity of the Latins, sufficiently examined what those same Orientals were contriving against the faith in that one will which they asserted, until Sophronius, Stephen, Maximus and other eminently catholic men, going to the aid of their Mother (Church) and the Syrians' snares having been exposed, spurred the most noble Roman prelates John IV, Theodore and Martin, splendidly, for the Roman see's supreme power in matters of faith, to finish off the hydra with sure blows; the business at last being brought to a happy end through the Lord, Agatho, Leo II and Constantine.

text: (i) Ἀλλὰ αὐτοβουλίαν. Emendo ex Sophronii Synodica, ταυτοβουλίαν· hoc enim est ἓν θέλημα, quod ipse exponit Maximus. Sic Sophronius Christi mysterium explicari dicit a Nestorio, ἰσοτιμίᾳ, ταυτοβουλίᾳ· pari honoris consortio, eadem voluntate, etc. Sic quoque sequenti tractatu de eodem, Ἐξ ἧς καὶ τὴν ταυτοβουλίαν συνίστησι, ἢ τὴν πολυβουλίαν, εἰπεῖν οἰκειότερον. Scite vero id, ταυτοβουλίαν, πολυβουλίαν, quod una illa Nestorii voluntas, solum affectu aut habitudine sit una, σχετικῶς: reipsa vero et natura personaque illi multiplex, uti se res in amicitia, qua sic unum dicimur ac unus, habet.
anchorLine: ἀλλὰ αὐτοβουλίαν (i), τουτέστιν, ἐν
en: (i) "Ἀλλὰ αὐτοβουλίαν." I emend, from Sophronius's Synodica, to ταυτοβουλίαν (sameness of will); for this is ἓν θέλημα (one will), which Maximus himself explains. So Sophronius says the mystery of Christ is explained by Nestorius as ἰσοτιμίᾳ, ταυτοβουλίᾳ: by an equal sharing of honour, by the same will, etc. So also in the following treatise on the same subject: "from which he also establishes the ταυτοβουλίαν, or rather the πολυβουλίαν, to speak more fittingly." And you rightly see this, ταυτοβουλίαν, πολυβουλίαν: that Nestorius's one will is one only in affection or habit, relatively (σχετικῶς); but in fact, in nature and person, it is manifold for him, as things stand in friendship, in which we are called one and the same.

text: (j) Περὶ θελημάτων δύο. Hunc tractatum primum refert ill. Annalium Pater, inter eos Maximi tractatus, quos spectare ad superiores illi numeratos non male forsitan conjicit. Videtur is, ad quem scribit, in monachi solum palæstra exercuisse, non vero sacerdotali, seu etiam episcopali dignitate fulsisse. Id certe Maximus ex more insinuasset, sic luculenter ad eum præfatus, ejusque tantis laudata eximia vitæ sanctimonia. Num hæc illa est, quam Stephano ἡγουμένῳ scriptam retulit Photius in ejus Epistolarum catalogo? Tenenda sententia, dum certioris aliquid monumenti prodeat. Luculenta certe epistola est, et inter Maximi dogmaticas non infima.
anchorLine: Περὶ θελημάτων β΄ (j) τοῦ ἑνὸς Χριστοῦ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἡμῶν.
en: (j) "Concerning two wills." The illustrious Father of the Annals lists this treatise first among those tracts of Maximus which he conjectures, not badly perhaps, belong to the numbers given above. The man to whom he writes seems to have exercised himself only in the monastic arena, and not to have shone in priestly or even episcopal dignity. Maximus would surely have hinted at this, as is his custom, having addressed him so fully, and praised his outstanding sanctity of life. Is this the letter that Photius reports in his catalogue of Epistles as written to Stephen the hegumen? The opinion is to be held until some more certain monument appears. It is certainly a splendid letter, and by no means the lowest among Maximus's dogmatic ones.

text: (k) Ὁ εὐλαβὴς πεποίηκε Μοναχός. Et hic nobis ignotus monachus, sic velut κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν dictus εὐλαβής. Non facile existimandus Sophronius, qui Maximo hæc scribente, vel jam episcopus erat, vel e vivis excesserat. Etiam Damascenus hanc laudat voluntatis naturalis definitionem.
anchorLine: ὁ εὐλαβὴς πεποίηκε μοναχὸς (k), εἰ εὖ ἔχει, ἢ μή,
en: (k) "The pious one has made (this) a monk." Here too a monk unknown to us, called as it were par excellence 'the pious one'. Sophronius is not easily to be supposed, who, when Maximus was writing this, was either already a bishop or had departed from the living. Damascene too praises this definition of natural will.
